newsitem.title: GERMANY: Upper house blocks protection for Stasi informers.
newsitem.headline: Upper house blocks protection for Stasi informers.

text.p: The upper house of the German parliament on Friday blocked an attempt to protect people who informed for East Germany's Stasi secret police by limiting an employer's right to know about their spying.
The lower house passed a bill earlier this month which would have offered some protection to ex-informers.
But the Bundesrat, which represents the 16 federal states, voted to keep the present system unchanged, meaning a compromise will have to be sought by an arbitration committee.

Many east Germans oppose attempts to rehabilitate those who kept the totalitarian Communist regime alive for over 40 years until 1990, including 175,000 citizens who spied informally for the Ministry of State Security (Stasi).

Christine Lieberknecht, Bundesrat representative for the east German state of Thuringia, said the bill passed by the lower house "amounts to a tacit amnesty for those who for years implemented discrimination in East Germany".

United Germany has until now screened east Germans to stop informers and Stasi employees getting jobs as civil servants, teachers or police, and employers have been entitled to get access to this information.
But many affected employees -- often only small-time informers who perhaps worked for the Stasi for only a few months -- have won court appeals against dismissal.
The bill acknowledged this by ruling that employers had no right to check up on their employees' Stasi record before 1976.

Regardless of the legal framework, there are signs that employers are becoming more ready to turn a blind eye to former Stasi involvement, particularly when the alternative is to gut large parts of east German public institutions.
In the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, two-thirds of the public servants exposed as Stasi informers still have jobs.
Proponents of the new bill say it will not prevent the Stasi's victims getting access to their files, noting that 15,000 people still file such requests every month.
